512.prompt: I opened the window and heard a distant bell. Beneath it, I could also hear
512.completion:
sporadic crashes and flashes of light in the sky. I guessed the bell had something to do with it, though I've heard this bell before, but never this close. Storm clouds were forming. I've never seen rain in the desert before, so I left my window open to take it in. At least it would be an act I could later recall, and perhaps write in my notebook. It was almost certain it would be new to me, and new to most I supposed.

There was a bit of rainfall. It was the first I'd ever experienced. Watching it, I thought, how would I describe it? If I had to put it down on the page, how would I tell it? Would I say that it was tiny water crystals falling from the sky, shining as they hit the window? Would I say that it was like pollen as it softly streamed down, carried on the wind? Was it a phenomenon as entrancing as snow?

512.prompt: From where I stood on the pier, I could see three boats entering the harbor. The nearest one
512.completion:
had a light boathouse that held five passengers. I had to squint to see them clearly. A boathouse was for docking in port without using a berth. When the person stepped down onto the pier, the boathouse glided back into the boat, smoothly filling the space where it had been docked and attaching mechanisms that prevented it from being a floating boat until it was maneuvered back into the water and the housings were released.

As the man neared, the inner lining of the boathouse turned from a translucent white into a mirror and the vessel ceased motion. I stepped slowly back as he stood outlined in the figure eight entry-ways. It was too much to hope that he was an emissary from Honest Abe, sending notice that he was riding in to save us all. The port regularly received some of these convictionalists, people who believed that the area of Kansas and a portion of Iowa remained slavery free. There was a sect of them in Kansas City as well, who lived in an encampment, just outside the settlement. Camp Jayhawk, they called themselves.

But then there was hope that this was not one of them. He wore dress shoes as polished as the ivory he carried and since the prow of his vessel indicated that he frequented Philadelphia when not tied to a dock, he was likely our escaped slaveholder. He continued his momentum forward along the pier, hand outstretched and eager.

He was quite tall and well dressed. He wore a lighter tan coat to match his pants, cinched with a vest that was a shade darker. His shined boots barely made a sound as they hit the wooden boardwalk. The same lace along his cuffs twisted around the buttons of his coat, the pocketed flaps in the front and the drawstrings of his breeches.

All I could do was watch as he closed the gap between us.

“I understand you are the slaveholder of this port, Mister —” I asked him from ten feet away.

“I’m afraid that instead, you are mistaken, sir,” he said, making a graceful sidestep to the right and placing his hat on a post. It was a sailor’s hat with a band that swooped down around the back of his neck that before now, I had only seen worn in a painting.

“I work for a company that specializes in procuring fresh cargo… which brings me to the purpose of my visit.” He smiled as he spoke, displaying boomingly white teeth that appeared larger than should be possible.
